subject: Lumenware private-deploy: ingress mode selection (peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN)

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly@redwood.ai>

Subject: Lumenware private-deploy: ingress mode selection (peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN)

Hi Nadia —

Thanks again for the call this morning. Per our discussion I pulled together the initial evaluation and a matrix that maps the three common ingress patterns (VPC Peering, PrivateLink / interface endpoints, and site-to-site VPN) against Lumenware’s requirements: low 99th-pct latency for interactive agents, strict PCI-scoped traffic separation, and a requirement to keep traffic egress on customer-managed links for auditability. See attached "connectivity-options-matrix.xlsx" and a quick draft topology diagram "topology-draft.png".

Quick summary / questions up front:
- Peering: lowest latency, good for intra-VPC traffic, but requires cross-account VPC routes and can be awkward for multi-region replication. Also limited if Lumenware needs to isolate different production tenants into separate VPCs.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): strong isolation and endpoint-level policies, works well for SaaS-style hosted endpoints with fine-grained control; likely easiest for meeting PCI scoping because we can avoid routing through our public internet.
- S2S VPN: easiest for customers with an on-prem gateway or for initial pilots; predictable for compliance review but higher and less predictable latency.

We’d like to propose a hybrid pattern for your pilot: PrivateLink for production traffic where tenant isolation and auditability are highest priority, plus a dedicated S2S VPN path for management/diagnostics and for any legacy on-prem systems you need to reach. For low-latency interactive workloads we can discuss an optional cross-VPC peering mesh inside a single region if you prefer sub-10ms 99th-pct.

Questions for you:
1) Can you confirm whether Lumenware requires all PCI-scoped traffic to never traverse third-party transit (i.e., must stay over customer-controlled links)?
2) Do you have any firm constraints on BGP or IP addressing changes on your side?
3) When would you like us to produce the SOW and network-runbook draft — end of next week ok?

Next steps from our side: Ben and Jordan will sketch a recommended topology with expected latency/cost trade-offs and an ops checklist for certificate/key rotation and audit logging.

Thanks,
Kimberly Park
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

Thanks Kim — this is helpful. Couple quick clarifications: we do need PCI traffic to remain on customer-managed links; that means any path that traverses public internet (even over TLS) will need an additional compensating control and a longer compliance review.

On BGP/addressing: our network team prefers not to change existing prefixes for the first pilot. We have a pair of static /24s we can dedicate for the Redwood integration. We also have an on-prem ASA that can terminate IPSec but the team prefers to avoid full-mesh peering unless latency absolutely requires it.

End of next week for SOW works for us — target 2026-09-23. For the pilot we expect one production VPC per tenant (three tenants) and a non-prod VPC.

Nadia

Kim/Jordan/Nadia —

Thanks for the context. I sketched the attached recommendation (peering-plink-vpn-recommendation.pdf) and summarized trade-offs below. This is written to align with Lumenware’s PCI constraint and avoidance of renumbering for the pilot.

Recommendation (pilot):
- Primary ingress: PrivateLink/interface endpoints (one endpoint per tenant VPC). Rationale: per-tenant isolation, endpoint-level policy controls, and traffic stays on cloud provider fabric (no public Internet). Meets PCI requirement because egress from their VPC to our endpoint can be controlled and audited on their side.
- Management/legacy: Dedicated IPSec S2S VPN from Lumenware on-prem to a management VPC in their account. Use separate static /24 for management flows so audit and routing remain separate from prod tenant traffic.
- Peering (conditional): Implement a single-region VPC peering to a Redwood transit VPC only if benchmarked 99th-pct latency for interactive agent calls shows >6ms improvement over PrivateLink for the busiest tenant. The peering path requires cross-account routing and explicit subnet route entries — adds operational surface but can be constrained to a small set of subnets to limit blast radius.

Ops checklist (high level):
- Certs/keys: rotate TLS certs for endpoints every 90 days; IPSec pre-shared keys rotated every 180 days with documented change window.
- Audit logs: flow logs and endpoint access logs should be forwarded to Lumenware’s centralized SIEM (their account); we will publish a JSON schema for events and a CloudWatch-to-Splunk connector example.
- Failover: if PrivateLink endpoint degrades, traffic can fail over to the S2S VPN for diagnostic sessions only; full cutover requires manual approval because VPN latency/control plane is different.

Estimated monthly cost (approx):
- PrivateLink endpoints (3 tenant endpoints + 1 non-prod): ~$1,100/month (data processing and endpoint-hour charges) based on 2TB/month aggregate.
- IPSec VPN (management): ~$250/month (gateway hours + data) 
- Peering: cost is mostly egress data transfer (if used) and operational setup; include a one-time integration effort ~ 8 engineer-hours.

Timeline to SOW draft: We can produce SOW + runbook by 2026-09-22 EOD to meet their 09-23 target if we get NDA/SOW scope confirmation by 2026-09-17. I’ll attach the recommendation PDF and a short set of benchmarks we’ll run if Nadia approves the conditional peering test.

Next actions for Nadia: confirm whether you want the conditional peering benchmark (we’ll need permission to run perf tests between a test agent in your VPC and our endpoint), and confirm the SOW approval window.

Ben Carter

Redwood Inference
